nodes.label: Britain
nodes.full: The manager of the Revolt: the McMahon promises, the monthly gold subsidy, the arms and the liaison officers — and, at the peace, the mandates, the Sharifian thrones, and the decision to abandon Hussein to Ibn Saud.
nodes.src: background — Kedourie, 'In the Anglo-Arab Labyrinth' (1976).

nodes.label: The Ottoman Empire
nodes.full: The power the Revolt was launched against: the Young Turk government that appointed Hussein, the army that built the railway and held Medina for two and a half years, and the caliphate abolished by its Turkish Republican successor in 1924.
nodes.src: background — Teitelbaum (2001).

nodes.label: France
nodes.full: The mandatory power for Syria: it crushed Faisal's Damascus kingdom at Maysalun in 1920 and took the coast and the interior that the Revolt had claimed.
nodes.src: background — James Barr, 'A Line in the Sand' (2011).

nodes.label: Ibn Saud
nodes.full: The ruler of Najd: subsidised by Britain alongside Hussein, and in 1924–25 the conqueror of the Hejaz and, from 1926, its king.
nodes.src: background — Gary Troeller, 'The Birth of Saudi Arabia' (1976).

nodes.label: The wider Muslim world
nodes.full: The Indian Khilafatists, the Egyptian government, the Shiʿi authorities and the Ottoman loyalists — all with a stake in who held Mecca, and the audience for the caliphate claim and the demolitions.
nodes.src: background — Kramer, 'Islam Assembled' (1986).

nodes.label: The railway and the Young Turks
nodes.full: The Hejaz Railway reached Medina in 1908; the same year the Young Turk revolution brought Hussein to Mecca as emir. Friction grew between the sharif's drive for autonomy and the new government's centralising reach.
nodes.src: William Ochsenwald, 'The Hijaz Railroad' (1980); the CUP–sharif tension in the Ottoman records.

nodes.label: Sharif Hussein bin Ali
nodes.full: Appointed emir of Mecca by the Young Turks as a supposedly pliable figure, Hussein consolidated his position, opened secret talks with Britain, proclaimed the Arab Revolt in June 1916, and had himself declared King of the Hejaz.
nodes.src: George Antonius, 'The Arab Awakening' (1938); Joshua Teitelbaum, 'The Rise and Fall of the Hashimite Kingdom of Arabia' (2001).

nodes.label: The Revolt and Hussein's sons
nodes.full: Faisal, Abdullah, Ali and Zeid led the Revolt's armies — the capture of Mecca, Ṭāʾif and Jeddah, the long siege of Medina, and the northern campaign with T. E. Lawrence to Aqaba and Damascus.
nodes.src: T. E. Lawrence, 'Seven Pillars of Wisdom' (1926); Faisal's and Abdullah's memoirs; Antonius (1938).

nodes.label: King Hussein isolated
nodes.full: After the war Hussein refused to ratify the peace treaties and the mandates because they did not recognise an Arab Palestine, lost the British subsidy, and in 1924 — after the Turkish Republic abolished the Ottoman caliphate — claimed the caliphate himself, to almost universal rejection.
nodes.src: Teitelbaum (2001); the Anglo-Hejazi treaty negotiations 1921–24.

nodes.label: The Saudi conquest and King Ali
nodes.full: Ibn Saud's forces took Ṭāʾif and Mecca in 1924; Hussein abdicated in favour of his son Ali and went into exile. Ali held Jeddah under siege for a year before it fell in December 1925, and Ibn Saud was proclaimed King of the Hejaz in January 1926.
nodes.src: Teitelbaum (2001); the contemporary press and the British consular reports.

nodes.label: The Hashemite thrones abroad
nodes.full: Faisal's brief Kingdom of Syria was crushed by France at Maysalun in 1920; the British then made him King of Iraq (1921), and gave Abdullah the Emirate of Transjordan (1921). The dynasty ruled everywhere but its Hejazi homeland.
nodes.src: the 1921 Cairo Conference; Ali A. Allawi, 'Faisal I of Iraq' (2014); Mary Wilson, 'King Abdullah, Britain and the Making of Jordan' (1987).

nodes.label: The government of the Kingdom of the Hejaz
nodes.full: A handful of Syrian and Hejazi officials ran the kingdom's small ministry, customs and Hajj administration on a British subsidy and the pilgrimage revenue. A constitution was promised in 1917 and never issued.
nodes.src: Teitelbaum (2001); Randall Baker, 'King Husain and the Kingdom of Hejaz' (1979).

nodes.label: The McMahon–Hussein bargain
nodes.full: The correspondence in which the British High Commissioner in Egypt promised support for Arab independence in exchange for a revolt against the Ottomans — its territorial extent, especially over Palestine and the Syrian coast, left studiously vague.
nodes.src: the McMahon–Hussein letters (July 1915–March 1916); Antonius, 'The Arab Awakening' (1938), which printed them; Elie Kedourie, 'In the Anglo-Arab Labyrinth' (1976).

nodes.label: The Revolt in the Hejaz
nodes.full: The Revolt was proclaimed at Mecca in June 1916; the city, Ṭāʾif and — with British naval support — Jeddah fell within months. Medina did not, and the failure to take it shaped the rest of the campaign.
nodes.src: Lawrence (1926); the British official history; Antonius (1938).

nodes.label: The siege of Medina
nodes.full: Fakhri Pasha held Medina for two and a half years, surrendering only in January 1919, months after the armistice — the last Ottoman force in Arabia, and a defence that became an Ottoman and Turkish legend.
nodes.src: the Ottoman accounts of the Medina defence; the deportation of the civilian population (the 'Sefer Berlik').

nodes.label: The northern campaign — Aqaba and the railway
nodes.full: Faisal's Northern Army, advised by T. E. Lawrence, took Aqaba from the desert side in July 1917, raided the Hejaz Railway for a year, and entered Damascus in October 1918 ahead of, or alongside, the British.
nodes.src: Lawrence, 'Seven Pillars of Wisdom' (1926); the debate over the Arab and Allied roles at Damascus.

nodes.label: Maysalun and the end of Faisal's Syria
nodes.full: The French ultimatum, the battle at Maysalun and the death of the war minister Yusuf al-ʿAzma, and the expulsion of Faisal from Damascus in July 1920 — the collapse of the Arab state the Revolt had been fought to create.
nodes.src: the French mandate records; Allawi, 'Faisal I of Iraq' (2014).

nodes.label: The Saudi–Hashemite war
nodes.full: The Ikhwān stormed Ṭāʾif in September 1924, with a massacre that emptied the town; Mecca fell in October; and the year-long sieges of Jeddah and Medina ended the Hashemite Hejaz by December 1925.
nodes.src: Teitelbaum (2001); the contemporary reporting.

nodes.label: The Hejaz Railway administration
nodes.full: The line was built and run by the Ottoman army on worldwide Muslim donations, with its own stations and pilgrim service. The political decision to stop it at Medina — the sharif's, and the tribes' whose caravan income it threatened — is why it never reached Mecca.
nodes.src: Ochsenwald, 'The Hijaz Railroad' (1980); Jacob Landau, 'The Hejaz Railway and the Muslim Pilgrimage' (1971).

nodes.label: The Kingdom of the Hejaz as a state
nodes.full: Hussein's attempt to build a government — a promised constitution, a small ministry, a customs, a Hajj administration, a coinage — on a British subsidy and the pilgrimage. It never developed the institutions of a durable state.
nodes.src: Randall Baker, 'King Husain and the Kingdom of Hejaz' (1979); Teitelbaum (2001).

nodes.label: Palestine and the treaties Hussein would not sign
nodes.full: Hussein refused to ratify the Treaty of Versailles, the draft Anglo-Hejazi treaty and the mandate arrangements because they did not recognise an Arab Palestine — a principled stand that isolated him diplomatically and cost him the British subsidy in 1920.
nodes.src: Teitelbaum (2001); the Anglo-Hejazi treaty drafts and Hussein's rejections.

nodes.label: The Baqīʿ demolitions and the first Muslim World Congress
nodes.full: The Ikhwān's second demolition of the domed tombs of the Baqīʿ and Muʿallāʾ cemeteries brought an outcry across the Muslim world; Ibn Saud convened a Muslim congress at Mecca in 1926 to manage the fallout and legitimise the new custodianship.
nodes.src: the contemporary Indian and Egyptian Muslim press; Martin Kramer, 'Islam Assembled' (1986), on the 1926 congress.

nodes.label: The Revolt and the idea of Arab nationalism
nodes.full: The Revolt was launched in the name of Arab independence and of Islam against a Turkish government the sharif called irreligious. It was the first time a large Arab movement fought under a national rather than a purely dynastic or tribal banner.
nodes.src: George Antonius, 'The Arab Awakening' (1938); C. Ernest Dawn, 'From Ottomanism to Arabism' (1973).

nodes.label: The caliphate question
nodes.full: The Turkish Republic abolished the Ottoman caliphate in March 1924; Hussein claimed it within days, to near-universal rejection, and a scramble followed — Egypt, Ibn Saud, the Indian ʿulamāʾ — over whether anyone could now hold the thirteen-century office.
nodes.src: Kramer, 'Islam Assembled' (1986); Mona Hassan, 'Longing for the Lost Caliphate' (2016).

nodes.label: Wahhābism returns to the Ḥaramayn
nodes.full: The Saudi conquest brought the doctrine back to the two holy cities permanently — the religious police, the ban on the mawlid and the tomb visitation, the demolition of the shrines, and the enforcement of the doctrine on the pilgrims of the whole world.
nodes.src: Teitelbaum (2001); David Commins, 'The Wahhabi Mission and Saudi Arabia' (2006).

nodes.label: The Khilafat movement and the global reaction
nodes.full: Indian Muslims, mobilised since 1919 to defend the Ottoman caliphate, watched the Hejaz change hands and the shrines fall. The loss of both Ottoman and Hashemite custodianship, and the demolitions, radicalised the Indian Muslim politics that later fed the Pakistan movement.
nodes.src: Gail Minault, 'The Khilafat Movement' (1982); Kramer, 'Islam Assembled' (1986).

nodes.label: The Hejaz Railway as monument
nodes.full: The stone stations, water towers, workshops and bridges of the line from Maʿān through the northwest oases to Medina — much of it wrecked in the Revolt and standing in the desert ever since, the largest engineering relic in northwest Arabia.
nodes.src: the surviving stations and rolling stock; the Saudi and Jordanian heritage surveys of the line.

nodes.label: The flag and symbols of the Revolt
nodes.full: The Arab Revolt flag of 1916 — black, white and green bands with a red triangle — is the ancestor of the flags of Jordan, Iraq, Syria, Palestine, Kuwait and others, and the seal and coinage of the short-lived kingdom carried the same claim to an Arab nationhood.
nodes.src: the Arab Revolt flag and its attribution to Sir Mark Sykes / the Arab officers; the Hejazi coinage 1916–25.

nodes.label: Lawrence and the image of the Revolt
nodes.full: T. E. Lawrence's 'Seven Pillars of Wisdom' and Lowell Thomas's lecture-and-film show made the Arab Revolt a Western romance and Lawrence a celebrity — a version that overshadowed the Arab account of the campaign for decades.
nodes.src: T. E. Lawrence, 'Seven Pillars of Wisdom' (1926); Lowell Thomas, 'With Lawrence in Arabia' (1924).

nodes.label: Old Jeddah under the siege
nodes.full: The coral merchant town held out for a year in 1925, its wall breached by Saudi artillery. Its surrender in December 1925 was the last act of the Hashemite Hejaz, played out in the city that had been the province's window on the world.
nodes.src: Ulrike Freitag, 'A History of Jeddah' (2020); the contemporary accounts of the siege.

nodes.label: The McMahon–Hussein Correspondence and the 'betrayal' debate
nodes.full: The letters of 1915–16, deliberately imprecise about Palestine and the Syrian coast, and the century of Arab, British and Zionist argument over exactly what territory was pledged to an Arab state and what was reserved.
nodes.src: Antonius, 'The Arab Awakening' (1938); Kedourie, 'In the Anglo-Arab Labyrinth' (1976); the 1939 British committee that failed to agree on the meaning.

nodes.label: Sykes–Picot and the Balfour Declaration
nodes.full: The secret 1916 Anglo-French partition of the Ottoman Levant, revealed by the Bolsheviks in 1917, and the 1917 British declaration of support for a Jewish national home in Palestine — the two documents that, set against the McMahon letters, define how the Revolt's participants read the settlement.
nodes.src: the Sykes–Picot map; the Balfour Declaration (2 November 1917); James Barr, 'A Line in the Sand' (2011).

nodes.label: The Arab and Ottoman accounts
nodes.full: The memoirs of the Revolt's Arab commanders and officials, and the Turkish accounts of the defence of Medina, have slowly balanced the Lawrence-centred Western narrative and restored the Arab and Ottoman participants to their own story.
nodes.src: Abdullah I of Jordan, 'Mudhakkirātī' (Memoirs); Suleiman Mousa, 'T. E. Lawrence: An Arab View' (1966).

nodes.label: The Hejaz on a British subsidy
nodes.full: Hussein's kingdom ran on a monthly British payment in gold sovereigns — for the Revolt and then to keep the pilgrimage roads open — plus the Jeddah customs and the Hajj. When the subsidy stopped in 1920, the state was insolvent within a few years.
nodes.src: Teitelbaum (2001); the British Treasury records of the Hejaz subvention.

nodes.label: The pilgrimage through war and conquest
nodes.full: The Hajj shrank drastically during the war and the Revolt, recovered in the early 1920s, and passed — administration, customs and all — to the Saudis in 1925, with barely an interruption to the season.
nodes.src: John Slight, 'The British Empire and the Hajj' (2015); the Hajj statistics for 1914–26.

nodes.label: The railway and the caravan economy
nodes.full: The line reaching Medina in 1908 collapsed the tribal and camel-broker income from the northern pilgrim route — a grievance that helped the Revolt recruit the tribes of the northwest to blow the railway up.
nodes.src: Ochsenwald, 'The Hijaz Railroad' (1980); the tribal opposition to the line.

nodes.label: The Hejaz Railway
nodes.full: Thirteen hundred kilometres of narrow-gauge line from Damascus to Medina, built in eight years by the Ottoman army and the German engineer Heinrich Meissner, cut the pilgrim journey from forty days to five — and was never extended the last four hundred kilometres to Mecca.
nodes.src: Ochsenwald, 'The Hijaz Railroad' (1980); Landau, 'The Hejaz Railway and the Muslim Pilgrimage' (1971).

nodes.label: The war of the railway
nodes.full: Armoured cars, aircraft, machine-guns and demolition charges came to northwest Arabia with the Revolt; Lawrence's railway raids and the Ottoman armoured trains were a small laboratory of mechanised desert warfare a generation before it went mainstream.
nodes.src: Lawrence, 'Seven Pillars of Wisdom' (1926); the Royal Flying Corps records for the Hejaz.

nodes.label: Britain, the Revolt and the promises
nodes.full: The McMahon letters, the gold and the arms, the liaison officers, and the parallel secret deals with France and the Zionists — Britain managed the Revolt as one instrument among several in its Middle Eastern war.
nodes.src: Kedourie, 'In the Anglo-Arab Labyrinth' (1976); the Arab Bureau records.

nodes.label: Paris, San Remo and the mandates
nodes.full: Faisal at the Peace Conference, the conditional Faisal–Weizmann agreement, the King–Crane Commission that was ignored, and the San Remo award of the mandates to Britain and France — the settlement that gave the Arabs almost none of what the Revolt had been promised.
nodes.src: Margaret MacMillan, 'Peacemakers' (2001); the San Remo resolution (April 1920).

nodes.label: The 'Sharifian solution' of 1921
nodes.full: At the 1921 Cairo Conference Britain settled Iraq on Faisal and Transjordan on Abdullah — placing the dynasty on thrones it had not won, in exchange for its acceptance of the mandate framework and of a reduced Palestine.
nodes.src: the Cairo Conference proceedings; Aaron Klieman, 'Foundations of British Policy in the Arab World' (1970).

nodes.label: Ibn Saud, Britain and the fall of Hussein
nodes.full: Britain subsidised both Ibn Saud and Hussein and brokered the tense peace after the 1919 Battle of Turaba; by 1924, at odds with Hussein over Palestine and the caliphate, it abandoned him — and did not lift a finger to stop the Saudi advance on Mecca.
nodes.src: Teitelbaum (2001); Gary Troeller, 'The Birth of Saudi Arabia' (1976).

nodes.label: The Muslim world's stake in Mecca
nodes.full: The Indian Khilafatists, the Egyptian government, the Shiʿi authorities and the Ottoman loyalists all had a stake in who held the holy cities; the 1926 Muslim congress was the first attempt to give the wider umma a formal say in the guardianship.
nodes.src: Kramer, 'Islam Assembled' (1986); the proceedings of the 1926 Congress of the Islamic World.

nodes.label: The Hejaz at the centre of the settlement
nodes.full: For one decade the western Arabian coast was where the future of the Arab east was decided — the Revolt launched there, the promises made to its king, and the borders of Syria, Iraq, Jordan and Palestine drawn against those promises.
nodes.src: MacMillan, 'Peacemakers' (2001); Barr, 'A Line in the Sand' (2011).

nodes.label: The last independent Hejaz
nodes.full: The Kingdom of the Hejaz was the only fully independent Arab state of its moment — and it lasted nine years, undone by its own isolation, its king's refusal to compromise on Palestine, and a stronger neighbour that Britain chose not to restrain.
nodes.src: Teitelbaum, 'The Rise and Fall of the Hashimite Kingdom of Arabia' (2001).

nodes.label: The thread ends — the Hejaz becomes Saudi
nodes.full: With the fall of Jeddah in December 1925 the Hejaz was joined to Najd, and in 1932 the two became the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia. The holy cities have been ruled from Riyadh ever since — the end of a thirteen-century thread of local Hejazi rule.
nodes.src: the Saudi–Hejaz union; saudi-1902-today carries the story forward. This closes the Hejaz thread of the atlas.

nodes.label: The tribes and the Revolt
nodes.full: The Bedouin of the Hejaz — the Ḥarb, the Juhayna, the Billī, the Ḥuwayṭāt — provided most of the Revolt's fighters, paid in gold and rifles, and their raiding tradition was what Lawrence's campaign harnessed, exploited and romanticised.
nodes.src: Lawrence, 'Seven Pillars of Wisdom' (1926); Joshua Teitelbaum on the tribal basis of the Revolt.

nodes.label: The people of the sieges
nodes.full: The civilians of Medina under two and a half years of Ottoman siege — famine, the forced deportation of much of the population, the eating of locusts — and of Jeddah under the Saudi guns in 1925, a year inside a wall being knocked down.
nodes.src: the accounts of the Medina 'Sefer Berlik'; Freitag, 'A History of Jeddah' (2020), on the 1925 siege.

nodes.label: Slavery at the end
nodes.full: The Kingdom of the Hejaz still had a slave market at Mecca; the League of Nations and the British pressed Hussein and then Ibn Saud on it. The Saudi state did not formally abolish slavery until 1962 — the institution outlived every regime in this folio.
nodes.src: Suzanne Miers, 'Slavery in the Twentieth Century' (2003); the League of Nations slavery commission reports.
